title: Refusal Prefix Concentration Under Role-Play Personas: Does a System-Prompt Persona Disrupt Shallow Alignment?

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: persona-based jailbreaks (DAN prompts) are among the most widely used attacks by non-technical users. Connecting them to the Qi et al. mechanistic finding (first-token refusal prefix disruption) bridges practical attacks with theory.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Accessible: inference-only experiment. Just vary system prompts across 3 conditions on 2 models. No adversarial optimization, no training, no custom code beyond prompting and counting refusal prefixes.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped: 2 models, 3 system-prompt conditions, measure prefix concentration and ASR using StrongReject prompts. Clear, compact experimental design easily completable within 30 hours.

novelty.reasoning: Partially addressed: both components well-studied individually, but the specific mechanistic intersection (persona -> refusal prefix disruption) is a novel contribution.

novelty_assessment.label: partially_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: The two constituent pieces are individually well-studied: Qi et al. (2024/ICLR 2025) established shallow alignment and first-token refusal prefix disruption, and persona-based jailbreaks are extensively documented (arxiv:2507.22171 shows persona prompts reduce refusal rates by 50-70%, RoleBreaker achieves 87.3% ASR). However, the specific mechanistic bridge — measuring whether persona prompts specifically disrupt the refusal prefix concentration identified by Qi et al. — has not been directly tested. The ICLR 2025 paper 'One Trigger Token Is Enough' and 'RAID: Refusal-Aware and Integrated Decoding' study refusal token dynamics but not under persona conditions specifically. The novelty lies in the intersection, but each component is well-characterized.
